The DAFS Teaching App is a small program that runs on your own laptop and opens
in your web browser. It walks you through the course's Python lessons: you read
a short explanation, write code in an editor, press **Run**, and get feedback
straight away.

This guide shows you how to install it, start it, and keep it up to date.

# What you need

- **Python 3.10 or newer.** Check which version you have by opening a terminal
  (see below) and typing:

  ```bash
  python --version
  ```

  If this prints `Python 3.10` or higher, you're fine. If it prints an older
  version or an error, install Python from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/)
  or install [Anaconda](https://www.anaconda.com/download) first.

- **A terminal.** This is where you type the commands in this guide.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Windows

Open the Start menu and search for **Anaconda Prompt** (if you installed
Anaconda) or **Command Prompt** (if you installed Python from python.org).

## macOS

Press `Cmd + Space`, type **Terminal**, and press Enter.

## Linux

Open your terminal application (often `Ctrl + Alt + T`).

:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## `python` or `python3`?
On some computers the command is `python3` instead of `python`. If `python --version` doesn't work, try `python3 --version`
and use `python3` everywhere in this guide.
:::

# Installing the app

Copy the command below into your terminal and press Enter:

```bash
python -m pip install https://github.com/JPvdP/dafs-teach/archive/refs/heads/main.zip
```

This downloads the app together with everything it needs (Streamlit, pandas,
NumPy and matplotlib). It can take a minute or two the first time.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why `python -m pip` and not just `pip`?
If you have more than one Python on your computer (for example Anaconda *and*
Python from python.org), `pip` and `python` can belong to different ones. The
installation then seems to work, but the app can't find its packages.
`python -m pip` always installs into the Python you get when you type
`python`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Already have Git installed?
You can also install it with Git, which does the same thing:

```bash
python -m pip install git+https://github.com/JPvdP/dafs-teach.git
```
:::

# Starting the app

In your terminal, type:

```bash
dafs-teach
```

After a few seconds your web browser opens a new tab with the app. If it
doesn't, look in the terminal for a line like
`Local URL: http://localhost:8501` and paste that address into your browser.

::: {.callout-important}
## Keep the terminal open
The terminal window is what runs the app. If you close it, the app stops
working in your browser. Leave it open (you can minimise it) for as long as
you're using the app.
:::

# Stopping the app

When you're done, stop the app **in the terminal**, not in the browser:

1. Go back to the terminal window where you typed `dafs-teach`, and click
   inside it.
2. Press **`Ctrl + C`** (also on a Mac: `Ctrl`, not `Cmd`).
3. The terminal shows `Stopping...` and then its normal prompt again. The app
   has now stopped. You can close the browser tab and the terminal.

On Windows you may be asked `Terminate batch job (Y/N)?`. Type `Y` and press
Enter. If nothing happens after `Ctrl + C`, wait a few seconds or press it a
second time.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Closing the browser tab does not stop the app
If you only close the browser tab, the app keeps running in the terminal. If
you then start `dafs-teach` again in a new terminal, you end up with **two
copies** of the app running at the same time. The second one opens on a
different address (`localhost:8502` instead of `localhost:8501`), and it's
easy to lose track of which tab belongs to which copy.

So: always stop the app with `Ctrl + C` before you start it again. And if you
just closed the tab by accident, you don't need to restart anything: type
`localhost:8501` in your browser's address bar to get back to the running
app.
:::

Your progress is saved after every exercise you run, so stopping the app never
loses any work.

# Using the app

## The first time: enter your name

When you open the app for the first time it asks for your name.

::: {.callout-warning}
Use your **full name exactly as it appears on Brightspace**, and always use
the same spelling. Your completion codes (see below) are linked to this name,
so a typo or a nickname means your codes won't match.
:::

## Working through a lesson

1. On the home page, pick a lesson and click **Open**. Lessons are numbered in
   the order we cover them in class.
2. Read the instructions, then write your code in the editor.
3. Click **▶ Run** to run your code. The app tells you whether your answer
   passes the checks.
4. Stuck? Click **💡 Show hint** to reveal hints one at a time. Use
   **👁 Solution** only as a last resort — you learn far more by trying first.
5. Click **Next →** to go to the next exercise. Use the sidebar to jump between
   exercises, or **← Home** to go back to the list of lessons.

Your progress is saved automatically on your own computer, so you can close
the app and carry on later where you left off.

## Getting your completion code

When you've finished **every** exercise in a lesson, open that lesson's card on
the home page and expand **🎓 Get completion code**. Upload this code to
Brightspace as proof you completed the module.

# Updating the app

New lessons are added during the course. When we announce an update, first
stop the app if it's running (see [Stopping the app]), then run:

```bash
python -m pip install --upgrade https://github.com/JPvdP/dafs-teach/archive/refs/heads/main.zip
```

Then start the app again with `dafs-teach`. Your progress is kept.

# Good to know

- **Where is my progress stored?** In a folder called `.dafs_teach` in your
  home folder. Nothing about you is uploaded anywhere.
- **A file called `output.csv` appeared on my computer.** Some exercises
  practise saving data to a file. Those files end up in the folder your
  terminal was in when you started the app (usually your home folder). They're
  harmless, and you can delete them.
- **Only you can open the app.** The app only accepts connections from your
  own computer, so classmates on the same Wi-Fi can't open it.
- **Anonymous progress reports.** After a weekly deadline has passed, the app
  may send your instructor an *anonymous* summary of how the class did on that
  week's exercises (for example, how many attempts an exercise took). Your name
  is never included. You'll see a small notice when this happens.
- **Settings from your instructor.** If your instructor asks you to set a
  variable such as `DAFS_TEACH_SECRET` before starting the app, follow their
  instructions exactly. If you haven't been told to, you don't need to do
  anything.

# Troubleshooting

**`dafs-teach: command not found`** (or "not recognized as an internal or
external command")
: The installation worked, but your terminal can't find the command. Start the
  app this way instead:

  ```bash
  python -m dafs_teach
  ```

**`No module named pip`**
: Your Python was installed without pip. Run `python -m ensurepip --upgrade`,
  then try the installation again.

**A permission error during installation** (`Permission denied`, `Access is
denied`, or `Could not install packages due to an OSError`)
: This often happens on laptops managed by the university, where you don't have
  administrator rights. Add `--user` to install the app just for yourself:

  ```bash
  python -m pip install --user https://github.com/JPvdP/dafs-teach/archive/refs/heads/main.zip
  ```

  If `dafs-teach` is then "not found", start the app with
  `python -m dafs_teach` (see above).

**`error: externally-managed-environment`** (Mac or Linux)
: Your Python is managed by Homebrew or by your Linux system, and it doesn't
  allow installing packages into it. Don't work around this with
  `--break-system-packages`. Instead, install Python from
  [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/) or install
  [Anaconda](https://www.anaconda.com/download), open a new terminal, and run
  the installation command again.

**`No module named dafs_teach`**
: The app was installed into a different Python than the one `python` starts.
  Install it again with `python -m pip install ...` (exactly as in
  [Installing the app]), then start it with `python -m dafs_teach`.

**An error saying Python 3.10 or higher is required**
: Your Python is too old. Install a newer version (see [What you need]) and try
  again.

**The browser shows "Connection refused" or the page stops responding**
: Check that the terminal running `dafs-teach` is still open. If not, start the
  app again.

**The app opens on `localhost:8502` (or 8503, …) instead of `localhost:8501`**,
or a message says **port 8501 is already in use**
: Another copy of the app is still running, probably in a terminal you
  forgot about or minimised. Find that terminal and stop it with `Ctrl + C`
  (see [Stopping the app]), or simply close all terminal windows. Then start
  the app again: it opens on `localhost:8501` once more.

**Something else?**
: Copy the full error message from the terminal and bring it to the lab
  session, or post it on the course forum on Brightspace.
